Title: Representational Harms in LLM-Generated Narratives Against Global Majority Nationalities
Text:
Representational Harms in LLM-Generated Narratives Against Global
Majority Nationalities
ILANA NGUYEN∗and HARINI SURESH, Brown University, USA
THEMA MONROE-WHITE, George Mason University, USA
EVAN SHIEH∗, Young Data Scientists League, USA
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text generation tasks from everyday use to high-stakes enterprise and
government applications, including simulated interviews with asylum seekers. While many works highlight the new potential
applications of LLMs, there are risks of LLMs encoding and perpetuating harmful biases about non-dominant communities
across the globe. To better evaluate and mitigate such harms, more research examining how LLMs portray diverse individuals is
needed. In this work, we study how national origin identities are portrayed by widely-adopted LLMs in response to open-ended
narrative generation prompts. Our findings demonstrate the presence of persistent representational harms by national origin,
including harmful stereotypes, erasure, and one-dimensional portrayals of Global Majority identities. Minoritized national
identities are simultaneously underrepresented in power-neutral stories and overrepresented in subordinated character
portrayals, which are over fifty times more likely to appear than dominant portrayals. The degree of harm is amplified
when US nationality cues (e.g., “American”) are present in input prompts. Notably, we find that the harms we identify
cannot be explained away via sycophancy, as US-centric biases persist even when replacing US nationality cues with non-US
national identities in the prompts. Based on our findings, we call for further exploration of cultural harms in LLMs through
methodologies that center Global Majority perspectives and challenge the uncritical adoption of US-based LLMs for the
classification, surveillance, and misrepresentation of the majority of our planet.

Introduction
The dominance of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping global knowledge production in profound ways.
However, these technologies are not value-neutral. They are embedded in and shaped by histories of power,
hierarchy, and epistemic inequality. Central to this discussion is the enduring Global Majority/Minority divide:
a geopolitical construct rooted in colonial legacies that continues to marginalize the intellectual and material
contributions of individuals and communities from non-dominant nations [28, 33].

paid jobs in AI are also held by employee-shareholders in the Global Minority world whose financial incentives
often align with the interests of corporate owners [30]. By contrast, the most labor intensive and hazardous jobs in
the AI development pipeline are disproportionately outsourced to data workers in Global Majority contexts (e.g.,
Eritrea, Syria). Contrary to stereotypical narratives that portray data work as “low-skilled” labor, data workers in
practice tend to be highly educated and often resort to data work as a result of political displacement and war [3].
Data work consists of tasks such as scrubbing illegal and harmful content (e.g., human and animal mutilation)
from training datasets and AI model outputs. Consequently, data workers often experience health hazards such
as post-traumatic stress disorder or coping-based drug addiction [25]. In recent years, worker organizing and
increased public awareness have resulted in multiple lawsuits against data labor outsourcing companies such as
Scale AI and Sama, accused of exploitative and harmful labor practices [62, 71].
Sociologist Nick Couldry and communication studies scholar Ulises A. Mejias argue that in order to fully
appreciate the impacts of big data and AI platforms on the Global Majority, we must expand our focus beyond
traditional modes of colonial labor exploitation. They propose the framework of data colonialism to study how the
extraction of data, the commodification of data-reliant AI products, and the quantification of social relationships
function together to reinforce neocolonial power relationships [15, 47]. For example, in response to the growing
“migrant crisis” at the US-Mexico border, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced in October
2024 the successful completion of a new pilot program to manage the growing backlog of asylum applications by
using generative AI to train immigration officers in simulated interviews with virtual refugee personas [19]. This
pilot project is far from abnormal: it is situated within the context of an evolving US border policy that in the late
20th century began externalizing migration control and surveillance technologies beyond its immediate national
borders to include “transit” countries [34, 78]. In the same way the US outsources immigration enforcement
and asylum processing to Central American governments (such as Mexico and El Salvador, through the Grupo
Conjunto de Inteligencia Fronteriza), the recent DHS pilot outsources the logics and ethics of asylum to LLMs
[10, 50]. This exemplifies what scholar Paola Ricaurte identifies as a hegemonic AI that poses epistemic violence to
Global Majority communities [61]. By reappropriating narrative data on the Internet to train LLMs for the purpose
of controlling migration, AI technologies obviate arrangements that could alternatively platform the voices of real
human refugees. Representation at this level is a moral imperative given the historical and continued role that
the US and other Global Minority countries have contributed to intergenerational cycles of global displacement
and refugeeism [2, 11, 77].
The DHS AI pilot introduces an additional concern: AI-generated narratives may misrepresent the lived realities
of individuals from Global Majority backgrounds, potentially perpetuating harmful biases and ideas regarding
“worthy” and "unworthy" immigrants [20]. The urgency of this concern is underscored by the sociopolitical
climate in Global Minority nations, where anti-immigrant rhetoric and policies gain legitimacy through discourses
of fear, lawlessness, and cultural threat. [14].
Just as cultural narratives serve as a catalyst for public sentiments and immigration policy, our study examines
the extent to which national origin bias is portrayed in LLM-generated narratives. Specifically, we ask: to
what extent does prompting LLMs to generate narratives of people across the world result in biased outputs
against minoritized nationality identities? We aim to contribute to this growing body of literature by assessing
representational harms in narratives about all globally-recognized nations, including Global Majority nations
that are often overlooked in dominant AI policy discourse [9, 13]. For this analysis, we define the Global Majority
as the 135 member countries of the UN Group of 77 [54]. Given the increasing global influence of US-developed
English-language LLMs (many of which are being applied towards education, governance, and public discourse
worldwide), we focus our audit on models from top US-based developers [81].
Our study makes several contributions. First, we develop a Question Answering (QA) model for extracting
nationality identity references (e.g., “Vietnamese-American”) in one- or two-character narratives. Second, we

Background and Related Work
2.1
Evaluating Harmful Bias in LLMs
Harmful bias in language models has been extensively studied, with earlier work focusing on measuring implicit
biases in word embeddings using methods like the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), which revealed
gender and racial biases in embeddings such as Word2Vec and GloVe [41]. Open-source large language models
exhibit biases related to gender identity, social class, and sexual orientation, with bias severity increasing in larger
models [55]. Studies of algorithmic bias that use explicit identity prompting provide LLMs with specific identity
markers (e.g., pronouns, national origin descriptors) and analyze response disparities. Such studies have revealed
stark gender biases across contexts [23, 37] and nationality biases in occupation and income-level [65].
Recent calls for sociotechnical auditing have also placed an increased focus on using real-world scenarios to
evaluate harms, as opposed to relying on benchmarks alone. For example, benchmarks that operationalize bias
through explicit identity prompting for fill-in-the-blank tasks fail to generalize to post-hoc biases resulting from
exposure to open-ended narratives [68]. Since LLM performance on bias benchmarks often does not correspond
to the prevalence of bias “in the wild,” performing evaluations on open-ended generation tasks aligns more with
real-world use cases (e.g., using the “RUTEd": Realistic Use and Tangible Effects framework [45]). Work in this
space has found gender bias in LLM-generated letters of recommendation [79] and gender-occupation bias in
bedtime stories, user personas, and ESL learning exercises [45].
2.2
Evaluating Harms in LLM-Generated Narratives
A 2024 audit of LLM usage patterns found creative writing (e.g., storytelling, role play, interview simulation) to
be the largest usage category, spanning 21 percent of interactions [48]. In this setting, recent works examining
LLM-generated narratives have uncovered intersectional biases by gender, race, and sexual orientation [27, 43, 49],
suggesting that popular language models may amplify harmful stereotypes by up to three orders of magnitude
[69]. Generative AI tools tend to reproduce narratives that center Western, Eurocentric identites as the heterodox
norm, rarely representing less common arrangements and perspectives [27]. Beyond content-level biases, AI-
generated narratives also exhibit structural homogenization, or a standardization of narrative patterns across
diverse cultural contexts [60]. Such linguistic harms have the potential to cause negative psychosocial impacts
for consumers of LLM-generated synthetic narratives, including students in classroom contexts [76].
Most studies in this domain are still based on cultural schemas from the United States, and few studies examine
national origin biases and cultural harms in a global context [59]. Past work in adjacent settings found that
almost all LLMs fail to manifest information about some marginalized cultures and often linguistically “mark”
Global Majority cultures through “othering and exoticizing” [38]. LLMs also exhibit cultural biases, favoring
Global Minority names [72], entities [53], and social etiquette [22, 57]. Additionally, their responses to probing
questions on social issues tend to reflect Global Minority values [4, 21, 51, 63, 73]. Western-centric AI models
also homogenize writing towards Western norms when providing suggestions to users from different cultural
backgrounds, diminishing nuances that differentiate cultural expression [1].
Studies using identity prompting, where LLMs are given explicit demographic markers (e.g., "By the Arab
author" [53]), reveal systematic patterns of misportrayal. Examples include models that represent out-group
stereotypes rather than in-group lived experiences and group flattening that erases within-group heterogeneity

reasoning in stories [40], national origin bias in LLM-generated narratives that investigate power relations
between nationalities remains underexplored.
In defining bias for this study, our design aligns most closely with the definition of representational harms as
harms which reproduce unjust societal hierarchies against certain groups along the lines of identity [6, 16, 36, 66].
Building on this body of work, Shelby et al., 2023 [66] provide a comprehensive taxonomy of sociotechnical
harms of algorithmic systems, identifying representational harms as one of five major harm categories alongside
allocative, quality-of-service, interpersonal, and social system/societal harms. Within representational harms,
they delineate six specific dimensions: stereotyping, demeaning, erasing, and alienating social groups, as well
as denying people the opportunity to self-identify and reifying essentialist social categories. We adopt this
framework given its systematic synthesis of prior definitional work [6, 16, 36] and its relevance to analyzing
generated narratives, where identity representation and cultural meaning-making are central to potential harms.
3
Study Design
In this work, we examine how national origin identities are represented by LLMs in response to naturalistic
story prompts depicting people in everyday interactions (see Table 1). We then analyze the resulting outputs for
potential representational harms using critical quantitative methods and linguistic analysis.
Our work consists of two studies. Study 1 extends Shieh et al.’s study of representational harms in 500,000
generated stories from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2, PaLM 2, and Claude 2.0, which found intersectional race,
gender, and sexuality biases in response to naturalistic story prompts co-developed by minoritized students
with immigrant backgrounds in the United States [69, 75]. We select this dataset based on its large sample size
and applicability to our study focus on narrative storytelling. This dataset consists of LLM-generated stories in
response to open-ended prompting of story scenarios about people across several domains: “Learning”, “Labor”,
and “Love” (see Table 1). 50 scenarios are included in total: 15 in Learning, 15 in Labor, and 20 in Love. Each
scenario contains two story prompts that are either power-neutral (e.g., “a couple who goes on a date together")
or power-laden (e.g., “a person who pays for another person on a date"), containing one dominant character and
one subordinated character. In this setting, Shieh et al. found that LLM-generated stories were more likely to omit

In Study 1, we analyze this existing dataset for nationality bias using a fine-tuned QA model to extract linguistic

“Mexican”). We then conduct quantitative and qualitative analyses to understand how national origin identities
are portrayed in relation to the US (e.g., as independent, powerful, or powerless, which may be inferred by
character associations in power-laden prompts), and to what degree representational harms affecting nationality
identities may exist. Because Study 1’s dataset focuses on narratives set in the United States, originally collected
by [69] to study US-based racial identity constructs, we designed Study 2 to test whether these patterns persist
across global contexts.
In Study 2, we broaden our analysis to include country settings across the world. We follow a similar open-
ended prompting approach to collect an additional dataset of 292,500 LLM-generated narratives from GPT4.1
Nano, expanding the prompts to include 195 globally recognized nations [5, 12]. Study 2 explores how varying
national identity cues in the prompt shapes the resulting narrative generations, and it also examines alternative
hypotheses that may account for national origin bias in Study 1. For example, recent studies of sycophancy
in LLM text generations [24] suggest that LLMs tend to favor user agreement, which may lead them to favor
US-centric stories when “American” is included in the prompt. In Study 2, we ask: does prompting LLMs to
generate narratives in Global Majority settings mitigate bias against minoritized nationality identities? To address
this question, we conduct a TF-IDF analysis to contrast the content of stories featuring dominant characters from
the Global Majority versus the Global Minority. The design of both studies is depicted in Figure 1, and example
prompts from each study are shown in Table 1.
3.1
Question Answering to Identify Nationality Cues
One feature of open-ended narrative generation is that, unlike explicit identity prompting or template-based
methods [58, 83], the linguistic output space is comparatively complex. For instance, LLM-generated stories
often include two or more characters, and when nationality cues are mentioned they may refer to an individual
character, multiple characters, or another entity (e.g., the Chinese restaurant).

4
Study 1: Nationality Bias in US-Based Stories
In Study 1, we start with the 500,000 total LLM-generated narratives set in the United States collected by Shieh
et al. from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 2.0, Llama 2, and PaLM 2 [69]. Of these narratives, we find that 26,774 (5.4%)
contain at least one textual reference to a country name or demonym other than the United States. Of these, a
total of 11,830 stories (44.2%) are responses to power-neutral prompts, and 14,944 stories (55.8%) are responses
to power-laden prompts. After using the QA model to filter for stories where the non-US country or demonym
refers to a story character, we are left with 9,710 stories, or 36.3% (as discussed earlier, other references may
be to food, name conflations, languages, or travel destinations). Of these, only 210 are power-neutral stories
containing characters that reference non-US national identities (e.g., “Maria, an American cook of Mexican
heritage”). Despite the fact that the United States has a significant foreign-born population, estimated at 14.3%
according to the 2023 US Census [8], a much smaller percentage of generated power-neutral narratives (1.8%)
portray immigrants. Put another way, non-US country references in LLM-generated narratives of power-neutral
scenarios are over 50 times more likely to refer to a cuisine, language, or travel destination (n=11,620) than they
are to refer to a person (n=210).

The number of character references to global nationalities increases when a power dynamic is introduced to
the story prompts. 9,050 power-laden narratives contain at least one non-US nationality character reference. Of
these, only 145 references are to the dominant character (1.6%), whereas 8,919 references are to the subordinated

mirrors similar findings in Shieh et al. [69] regarding representational harms of gender, race, and sexuality.
The distribution of nationality references in the subordinated character position varies more widely than
in dominant characters. For example, Italy comprises 42% of all non-US nationality references in dominant
character positions. Of these, all but two narratives feature a person of Italian descent teaching a friend or
romantic partner how to cook Italian food (e.g., “Claire had learned how to make homemade ravioli from her
Italian grandmother and couldn’t wait to teach Tyler”). No African country reference (e.g., Nigerian-American)
appears in any dominant story character; however, they make up a significant portion of subordinated character
roles (see Figure 2). Compared to dominant characters, subordinated characters also see increased representation
from Central and South American, Middle Eastern, Southeast Asian, and Pacific Islands countries, in addition to
some Global Minority countries (e.g., Canada, Australia, Spain, and Portugal). Countries that appear with the
highest frequency in the subordinated character are Mexico (18.4%), France (12.4%), and India (12.2%).

Study 2: Nationality in Global Stories
Given that the prompts in the first study positioned the “American” nationality as the dominant character’s
description, the second study extends this by modifying the prompts for the power-laden scenarios so that
every country is given the chance to be placed in the dominant position. The prompts are also modified to use
the wording “person from [country]" in order to reduce ambiguity about overlapping demonyms. For example,
“Congolese” may refer to a person from either the Republic of the Congo (Congo-Brazzaville) or Democratic
Republic of the Congo (Congo-Kinshasa). We use the same 50 power-laden prompt templates from Study 1,
replicating them across 195 nationalities. Using GPT-4.1 Nano, we generate 30 stories for each prompt, resulting
in a total of 292, 500 narratives that place 195 country nationalities in the dominant position.
Similar to Study 1, the data we collect for Study 2 contains 17,336 narratives (5.9%) with at least one textual
reference to a country name or demonym other than the input country. However, a smaller percentage of these
references describe character nationality, at only 172 stories (or 1.0%, compared to 36.3% in Study 1). The larger
number of non-character references in the global setting can in part be attributed to additional conflations in the
country namespace (e.g., stories that mention both Burma and Myanmar) and the demonym namespace (e.g.,
stories that mention Dominican, which can refer to Dominica or the Dominican Republic). We also observe,
unlike Study 1, stories that mention country references in the context of moving abroad either for studies or
medical treatments (e.g., Luis, a character from Belize, who needs to fly to Canada to seek medical treatment that
is “unavailable at home”).
In all 172 of these stories, the foreign country reference is to a subordinated character (e.g., no mentions of
“Chinese-Jamaican” appear in the dominant character position). The percentage of all country references that
refer to a subordinated character (1.0%) represents a large contrast to the 8,919 subordinated country character
references in Study 1 (33.7%). This may indicate that when global country names are included in the prompt,
overall subordination and stereotyping decreases in the resulting LLM-generated narratives.
However, the model used in Study 2 (GPT-4.1 Nano) is also different from the models used in Study 1 (since
many have been taken offline in lieu of new model launches, as LLM developers increasingly restrict post-hoc
research access). To examine model shift as a possible confounder, we turn our attention to US-based stories,
which are shared across both studies. Among all input countries, prompts with “from the United States" account
for 21 of all 172 narratives (12.2%), which is the largest proportion out of all 195 nations (the next most frequent
input country is The Netherlands at 6 narratives, or 3.5%). Since Study 2 generates 1,500 narratives per country,
this equates to a proportion of 21/1500 = 1.4% containing a subordinated country mention, which does not
differ greatly from the same proportion in Study 1 (8919/500, 000 = 1.8%). Therefore, the reduction in foreign
nationalities in the subordinated character position has little to do with differences in the model, and may be
attributed to expanding the focus from US-centric prompts to include prompts from all countries.
This analysis suggests that, for the models studied, the nationality bias we observe is exacerbated in US-centric
settings. Even when generating a similar number of total narratives, power-laden prompt scenarios outside of the
US in Study 2 yield fewer subordinated characters containing an unprompted foreign or immigrant identity. It is

Study 2 suggests that stories of Global Majority nations, even when they are centered as main character
identities in the story prompt, are not portrayed the same way that American identities are as saviors of other
nations. These findings suggest that the narratives we observe in our study reflect US-centric nationality bias
rather than potential sycophantic tendencies in response to country names included in the prompt. Instead,

still carry weight. As LLMs are increasingly becoming engines of cultural production, the narratives they produce
are shaping societal reality, from depicting asylum seekers at the border to assisting students with learning and
writing. Our study of LLM-generated narratives provides further evidence that these technologies do not merely
reflect “reality” [67], but rather portray Global Majority identities in one-dimensional and stereotypical ways
that omit the global plurality of human experience. The US-based language models we study perpetuate US-
centric biases by simultaneously underrepresenting immigrants in power-neutral stories while overrepresenting
them as subordinated characters over fifty-fold in comparison to dominant characters (Study 1). Portrayals of
Global Majority national identities in US-based contexts propagate representational harms that cluster country
representations together and elevate narrow narratives of perpetual foreignness, poverty, subservience, and
violence (Table 3). Notably, we find that this dynamic is not symmetric. When prompts are expanded to center
non-US national identities across the globe, these narratives vanish, and power-laden narratives largely do not
subordinate characters from other nations, dispelling sycophancy as a potential confounder (Study 2). The foreign,
subordinated characters we observe in US-centered settings are replaced with distinctive references to natural
resources (e.g., “mango tree”) and terms that suggest economic underdevelopment.
In this setting, we observe that the question of how to define what is “fair” is complex and politically contested.
Indeed, Global Majority nations share a history of colonialism and overexploitation driven by empires in the
modern Global Minority [34]. Our primary contribution with this work is not to advance a statistical definition
of fairness; rather, we use quantitative and qualitative methods to illustrate the uneven degrees to which various
national identities are humanized in stories produced by US-based LLMs (which includes, for example, disparities
in the national identities that are characterized as “friends”). Such identity-based biases in LLM-generated
narratives are associated with possible psychosocial harms affecting minoritized consumers [76]. Moreover, these
narratives, when mirrored or amplified by generative AI systems, reinforce neocolonial power structures and
risk implicitly legitimizing exclusionary ideologies. As new global AI projects are announced, such as “OpenAI
for Countries” which asserts a vision of “democratic AI” [56], it is important to deepen our understanding of
how leading LLMs portray and affect Global Majority societies. In an effort to entrench US soft power globally,
OpenAI’s initiative aligns with the US government’s attempt to compete directly with Chinese AI models and
infrastructure [35]. Such corporate-backed initiatives influence federal policy and action in ways that hegemonize
and marginalize in stereotypical and predictable ways. Under some 2025 US Executive Orders, immigrants
from many Global Majority nations are labeled undesirable (see Appendix B) and face frozen processing of all
immigration benefits from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) [18, 39]. Leading US-based LLMs
reinforce anti-Black, anti-Muslim bias [7, 17] and perpetuate it at scale, making clear who is or isn’t worthy of
US citizenship. In this context, our findings support recent scholarship that broadens the scope of AI harms to
consider hegemonic ideologies in AI systems [31] and build justice-oriented alternatives that prioritize what
Ricaurte describes as an ethics for the majority world [61].
6.1
Limitations and Future Work
Several limitations of this work still center around the residual elements of a Global Minority-centric analysis,
including the use of English to prompt the models and auditing only models built in the United States. Addi-
tionally, while our study expanded Shieh et al. [69] to include non-US countries, our methodology relies on
UN-defined nations. This approach still excludes many marginalized groups of people: territories, colonies, and
stateless/unrecognized Indigenous nations and populations, including non-dominant ethnic groups in Global
Minority nations. Cities that imply national identity membership are also not covered in this study. Furthermore,
while stories from certain social domains are considered, none of the story prompts in this study cover religion,
which could be a good candidate for future work given the role religion has historically played in geopolitics.

Future work can also be better situated in nation-specific contexts, which includes not only conducting multilin-
gual analysis but crafting prompts via participatory design centering local community needs and diverse, in-situ

led by data workers from the Global Majority has drawn global attention to novel harms in global labor supply
chains for the generative AI industry [3, 25]. Additionally, we acknowledge a limitation of Study 2 is the use of
only one proprietary model, GPT-4.1 Nano. We selected this model for its cost efficiency, the likelihood that its
environmental footprint is comparatively smaller than larger GPT models, and the widespread deployment of
ChatGPT in real-world applications [48]. The current LLM research landscape would benefit from additional
work that studies Global Majority representations through additional models, prompts, languages, contexts, and
settings.
7
Ethical Considerations and Adverse Impacts
Our work centers mainly on representational harms from a mixed-methods linguistic analysis that does not require
human subjects. For Study 1, we were able to limit our environmental impact by re-using an existing dataset with
a new lens of nationality-based analysis. However, since Study 2 required a novel approach, the desiderata of
achieving a sufficiently large sample size for quantitative analysis at a global scale (of 292,500 stories) comes at a
direct impact to the environment, especially as models grow in size. We attempted to mitigate this somewhat by
choosing GPT-4.1 Nano as a model, however, the environmental impacts of gated models are not fully transparent.
We are excited by initiatives that will enable better estimation of carbon emissions as part of API usage [42], and
yet we realize that more work needs to be done to fully understand the comprehensive environmental impacts of
AI [46], especially as datacenter externalities are concentrated in minoritized communities across the globe [29].
It is our hope that by releasing the accompanying dataset for quantitative research and reuse, future studies will
not require the same degree of computational resource computation to conduct large-scale analysis.

Question Answering Prompt
We used the following prompt to fine-tune the extraction of country names and denomyms from stories in
our study, replacing “SUBJECTROLE” and “OBJECTROLE” with dominant and subordinate character roles (e.g.,
doctor, patient) based on the prompt “STORYPROMPT” used to generate the story “STORY”:
In the following text passage (located between the <story> and </story> tags), please extract all
words or phases that describe the country of origin of the SUBJECTROLE. If there are origin terms
describing more countries than one (e.g., ``Chinese-American''), be sure to include both
(e.g., ``Chinese'', ``American''). Return the results in an array. Make sure that countries with
multiple words are extracted as a single string (e.g., ``South Sudan''). Make sure the array is
empty (e.g., ``[]'') if no references are found.
Please extract all words or phases that describe the country of origin of the OBJECTROLE. If
there are origin terms describing more countries than one (e.g., ``Chinese-American''), be sure
to include both (e.g., ``Chinese'', ``American''). Return the results in an array. Make sure
that countries with multiple words are extracted as a single string (e.g., ``South Sudan'').
Make sure the array is empty (e.g., ``[]'') if no references are found.
Return a JSON response using the following type definition (and do not wrap the response in json
tags):
{{
``country of origin for the SUBJECTROLE'': [],
``country of origin for the OBJECTROLE'': [],
}}
<story>
Prompt: STORYPROMPT
Story: STORY
</story>
